newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - Vietnam villagers vow to fight on in land dispute.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Vietnam villagers vow to fight on in land dispute.

text.p: Riot police haven't returned to Tho Da village. Not since they were beaten back with sticks and stones by hundreds of angry men, women and children last month.
Not yet.

"We will fight again," cries an old woman from the back of an animated crowd standing at the entrance to this village on the northern edge of Vietnam's capital, Hanoi. "This is our land, and the people are ready to sacrifice their lives for it."
The villagers of Tho Da grudgingly accept that rice fields which they and their ancestors have lived off for centuries will soon be turned into a swank, 18-hole golf course.
But they are determined to get "fair" compensation before the bulldozers of the project developer, a joint venture between South Korea's giant Daewoo Group and a local partner, move in.
The Tho Da villagers' wrangle with the authorities, whose job it is to dole out compensation, has erupted into ugly clashes with security forces twice in the past year.
Last May, one woman was killed and scores were injured when police began ripping up rice plants. Four people were jailed for their part in that violence.

Dozens were hurt again on December 30 when police, wielding electric prods and tear gas, fought a pitched battle on a new access track cutting through the fields. The villagers torched a truck and other vehicles to stop the track from being completed.
Where the track runs out, they have erected a signboard. "Dangerous Area. Do not Enter," its message reads above a crudely-painted skull and crossbones.
Public demonstrations rarely flare in communist Vietnam. When they do, they are rapidly put down and almost never reported in the tightly-censored press.
This latest one has been blacked out in the official media and local authorities say nothing untoward has happened at all.

However, many fear that disputes like the one at Tho Da will happen again and again as economic development brings a clash between the communist tenet that all land belongs to the state and the peoples' generations-old sense of collective land ownership.

"The biggest concern is whether this is just a one-time trouble...or whether it will occur again with other groups, at other factories," said Han Jeong-hyun, Hanoi Director of the KOTRA, a Seoul government trade and investment promotion agency.
South Korea ranks fifth in a growing list of countries which have companies investing in Vietnam's burgeoning economy and Daewoo is the biggest single investor.
After a run of critical press reports about South Korean firms mistreating employees in Vietnam, Daewoo is taking no chances.
As Daeha -- the joint venture which will build the golf course as part of a $177 million project -- stonewalled enquiries last week, Daewoo's chairman himself arrived, unannounced, in Hanoi.
The Hanoi Moi daily quoted Kim Woo-choong as assuring the Hanoi People's Committee chairman that the golf project was not just for golfers.
"The residents in that area will have a new life in the future through Daewoo's development of local human resources," he said.
Daeha says it struck a deal with the government on compensation for the farmers, and it is now up to the local authorities to pay out.

The company says it has not increased the compensation agreed in its package, which makes the villagers suspicious when their original offer of about $240 per household-plot of land was suddenly bumped up to about $726 after a clash with the police.

"We want the money we are supposed to get according to the government decision. With the amount they have offered us, we cannot live," says one of the villagers, a barefoot woman with a child in her arms.

The people of Tho Da, who dare not venture out of their settlement for fear of being arrested, say they want the dispute to end. They say Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, or at least a high-ranking government official, should intervene.
